tagline: Lake roads and canal towns follow an old corridor of forts and trade.
intro: Lakes to Locks Passage connects Rouses Point and Waterford through the Champlain Valley and eastern Adirondacks, with part of the drive beside the Champlain Canal. Lake roads, small cities and rural hamlets give the journey its changing scale. FHWA designates it an All-American Road and presents its interconnected waterways as the central attraction. The agency suggests two to five days to enjoy the New York byway.

The present byway grew from two earlier projects. New York designated the Champlain Trail a scenic byway in 1992. By early 2000, communities along the trail and the Champlain Canal had completed management plans. The state advisory board recommended merging their management that May; All-American Road designation followed in 2002. Lakes to Locks Passage, Inc., now manages the byway to preserve and promote its natural, cultural, recreational and historical resources. Along the corridor, 32 designated Waypoint Communities provide local attractions and services, with museums and other sites serving as Heritage Centers.

Heading south from Rouses Point, the highway route uses NY 9B to Chazy, U.S. 9 to Keeseville and NY 22 toward Whitehall. Between Westport and Ticonderoga, NY 9N follows Lake Champlain’s western edge. Fort Ticonderoga occupies a narrows near the lake’s southern end. At Whitehall, the journey meets the Champlain Canal, then continues south on U.S. 4 to Waterford.

moments.title: Rouses Point
moments.text: At Rouses Point, a border survey stopped a fort already under construction. Work began in 1816 to guard against attack from British Canada. A new survey placed the site in Canada, and builders abandoned the unnamed fortification. Residents salvaged its materials for houses and public buildings. The 1842 Webster–Ashburton Treaty brought Island Point into the United States, allowing construction of a second fort, Fort Montgomery, to begin in 1844. The two forts occupied the same site. Much of Fort Montgomery was demolished in 1936–1937, its crushed stone used as fill for a bridge between Rouses Point and Alburg, Vermont.

moments.title: Fort Ticonderoga
moments.text: Fort Ticonderoga controlled the carrying route between Lake George and Lake Champlain, beside the rapids of La Chute River. The French began building the star-shaped Fort Carillon in 1755. British forces took it in 1759, and troops led by Ethan Allen and Benedict Arnold captured it in May 1775. After the 1775 capture, Henry Knox transported many of its cannons to Boston to support the siege there. After its military use ended, residents stripped out usable building materials. The Pell family’s restoration opened to the public in 1909. The powder magazine is a later reconstruction, completed in 2008 using the original plans in part.

moments.title: Whitehall
moments.text: Whitehall’s canal-facing Main Street took shape after a fire in 1864. Its historic district contains three blocks of two- and three-story brick and stone commercial buildings facing the Champlain Canal. The canal reached Whitehall in 1823, adding another transport connection to a place already known for shipbuilding. During the Revolution, Benedict Arnold worked under Philip Schuyler to build a fleet here to confront British forces at Valcour Island. In 1960, New York’s legislature declared Whitehall the birthplace of the United States Navy. Local architect Almon Chandler Hopson designed most of the historic district’s buildings.
moments.notice: Look for the brick and stone commercial buildings facing the Champlain Canal.
